title: Allocation pressure and latency
description: Identify allocation patterns that drive GC pressure, understand how latency modes work, and reduce pause times in latency-sensitive applications.

data.text: GC pressure is the rate at which your application allocates objects on the managed heap. High allocation pressure forces the GC to run more often, which means more pause times — moments when the runtime stops your application code to reclaim memory. In a web service, these pauses add up to slower response times and lower throughput. In a real-time application, a single 50-millisecond GC pause can cause a dropped frame or a missed deadline. Understanding allocation pressure is the first step to writing predictable, low-latency code.

Not all allocations are equally harmful. An allocation of a tiny object that becomes unreachable within the same method is cheap — it is reclaimed in the next gen 0 collection in microseconds. An allocation of an object that lives for seconds and holds references to other long-lived objects is expensive — it promotes to gen 1 and then gen 2, making future collections more expensive. The goal is not zero allocations; it is allocations that do not survive long enough to cause problems.

Before you can reduce allocation pressure, you must measure it. `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread()` returns the total bytes allocated on the current thread since it started. `dotnet-counters` shows the allocation rate in bytes per second. PerfView can capture ETW events and produce a GC allocation stack trace that shows exactly which methods are allocating the most memory. The ETW event `GC/AllocationTick` fires for every allocation above a configurable threshold and includes the call stack.

data.title: Using dotnet-counters to monitor allocations
data.code:
# Monitor allocation rate in real time
dotnet-counters monitor --process-id 1234 \
  System.Runtime

# Sample output:
# % Time in GC        : 2.345%
# Allocation Rate     : 12.5 MB/s
# GC Heap Size        : 256 MB

# PerfView: capture a 30-second trace
PerfView collect -providers "Microsoft-Windows-DotNETRuntime:0x2000:5" \
  -maxCollectSec:30 \
  -stackWalkDepth:50

items: **String concatenation in loops** — `string` is immutable; `+=` in a loop allocates a new string on every iteration. Use `StringBuilder` instead.
**LINQ query overhead** — LINQ methods like `Select`, `Where`, and `OrderBy` allocate enumerator structs and closures. For hot paths, hand-written loops are allocation-free.
**Task.FromResult in tight loops** — `Task.FromResult` returns a cached completed task for value types but may allocate for reference types.

**Async/await state machines** — every `async` method that does not complete synchronously allocates a state machine object. Configure `ValueTask` or `IValueTaskSource` for high-frequency async paths.
**Boxing in generic code** — `where T : struct` constraints do not prevent boxing if you cast to `object`, `Enum`, or `IComparable`.

data.text: Reducing pause times with latency modes

When you cannot eliminate allocations entirely, you can use GC latency modes to control when collections run. The `LowLatency` mode suppresses background GC for the duration of a time-sensitive operation. It is useful for rendering frames, processing audio buffers, or handling network packets. The trade-off is that memory usage grows during the low-latency window. If you exceed the available memory, the runtime may throw an `OutOfMemoryException` or force an blocking collection.

data.title: LowLatency mode around a critical section
Measure % Time in GC before and after
data.text: The `% Time in GC` counter from `dotnet-counters` tells you what fraction of wall-clock time the application spends paused in GC. A value under 5% is healthy for most server applications. If you are above 10%, you have meaningful allocation pressure that is costing throughput. Before refactoring, capture a trace with PerfView, identify the top allocating methods, and then apply targeted fixes.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Allocation pressure is the rate of heap allocations; high pressure increases GC pause times and reduces throughput.
Measure allocations with `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread`, `dotnet-counters`, or PerfView before optimizing.
String concatenation, LINQ in hot paths, and async state machines are common allocation-heavy patterns.
GCLatencyMode.LowLatency suppresses background GC for critical sections, but watch for memory growth.
